Programming & interpretation · 2021

Thinking Like Transformers

Gail Weiss, Yoav Goldberg, and Eran Yahav

A programming language for reasoning about transformer computation.

Read the paper ↗Companion video ↓

The idea, briefly

The paper introduces RASP, the Restricted Access Sequence Processing language. It turns elements of transformer-encoder computation into primitives that can be composed into understandable programs.

Examples include histograms, sorting, and Dyck languages. The abstraction lets readers connect a task's program to the attention heads and layers needed to express it.

Editorial overview based on the paper’s abstract. Reading suggestions below are editorial guidance.

Why spend time here?

For thinking through a transformer algorithm as a program you can inspect, one step at a time.

A way into the paper

  • Work through a small RASP program with a short input sequence before moving to a larger example.
  • Notice which operations are sequence-wise computations and which select information from other positions.
Keep in mind

A hand-written program is an abstraction of a possible computation, not evidence that every trained transformer uses that program.
